strengths: R2E offers a technically coherent approach to evidence-based entity ranking. Candidate-specific retrieval, permutation-invariant evidence aggregation, and NULL-feature training provide a principled basis for attributing predictions to retrieved passages with Shapley values. The contribution is relevant to NLP retrieval and interpretability.

The entity-ranking experiments support useful improvements. On Gene Description Facts, even uncorrected R2E improves MRR to 0.202 versus 0.176 for MCS and 0.167 for MLM. Updating the retrieval corpus improves 2022 literature MRR from 0.205 to 0.219 without retraining, directly supporting the adaptability claim.

The biomedical evaluation includes a substantial clinical benchmark and a meaningful genetics baseline. R2E using templated genetics achieves 0.579 AUROC versus 0.545 for the ontology-based baseline, supporting the usefulness of language-based matching between related disease concepts.

The manuscript provides extensive architectural details, hyperparameters, attribution pseudocode, annotation prompts, ablations, and dataset construction procedures, and reports releasing three evaluation datasets. Document-level splits and training from scratch strengthen the temporal controls for the literature experiments.
weaknesses: End-to-end reproducibility remains a decisive concern. The paper explicitly withholds training data, code, and model weights, while relying on licensed literature and proprietary entity linking. The detailed appendices make the architecture implementable, but the released evaluation sets do not enable reproduction of the reported results. A reproducible public-corpus configuration or accessible trained system would substantially strengthen the case for Findings.

The comparisons do not fully isolate R2E's contribution. Frequency correction substantially improves R2E, but corresponding corrected MLM results are absent despite Appendix G deriving that correction. Clinical AUROC is also nearly identical for literature-only R2E and MLM: 0.632 versus 0.630. These results support competitive performance with attribution, but provide limited evidence of predictive superiority over the strongest textual baseline.

The explanation evaluation is narrower than the broader interpretability claims. Shapley values attribute the score conditional on the retrieved evidence set, but agreement with GPT-4 relevance labels does not establish reliable biological reasoning or improved expert decisions. Human validation covers only eight query–target pairs per task, with 512 evidence sentences each. Direct evaluation against human labels, comparison with retrieval-score attribution, and within-query evidence-ranking results would provide stronger support.

The clinical results require clearer qualification. The pre-2005 controls apply to literature, but no equivalent cutoff is documented for the genetics dataset assembled in 2023; the GPT-4 audit also introduces knowledge outside those controls. Consequently, the combined and audited configurations are not established as temporally clean historical predictions. Additionally, discontinued development is an acknowledged noisy proxy for efficacy failure, so conclusions should distinguish program outcomes from biological efficacy.

There is an unresolved numerical inconsistency: Table 3 reports 0.632 AUROC for literature-only R2E-Corrected, whereas Table S8 reports 0.639 for the apparently corresponding standard-training configuration. This discrepancy exceeds the reported auditing improvement of 0.005. Although the audit includes a DeLong significance test, uncertainty estimates and repeated-run results are missing for other key comparisons. Reconciling these results and strengthening the controlled evaluations are necessary for a clear positive recommendation.
